genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a neighbourhood drop-in centre
she grew up next door to a noisy workshop
quarrels between neighbours marked her childhood
she decided to face conflicts instead of avoiding them
she began by listing the causes of dispute
she set up a weekly drop-in session
so many people came that the room grew cramped
the local authority granted her a larger space
she puts her success down to experience, not to an inborn gift
text: From a glazed office looking onto the courtyard, the woman who runs a neighbourhood drop-in centre watches the families come and go. Her way of working grew out of her own life. As a child she lived in a flat that shared a wall with a noisy workshop, and the quarrels between neighbours left a lasting mark on her. Once grown up, she chose to take conflict head on rather than walk away from it. Knowing those everyday grudges from the inside, she began by listing every reason people fell out, then opened a drop-in session once a week. Families arrived in such numbers that the room was soon too cramped to hold them. That turnout persuaded the local authority to hand over a far larger space nearby. None of it, she insists, comes down to some gift she was born with: she simply turned an old wound into a useful skill.

units: the covered hall has recently been converted
the designers wanted an open volume with no partitions
the din of the stalls disturbs those who come to read
children moving about unsettle users looking for quiet
thick curtains hung on rails now divide the space
these dividers can be shifted as needs change
the work cost little and built nothing permanent
the writer judges this correction better than the original scheme
text: You step into the converted hall as into a sentence that runs on too long: the eye hunts for something to rest on and finds nothing. The flaw shows from the threshold, before you have even crossed the first row of stalls. The designers wanted one unbroken volume, with no partitions, where every use would mingle with the rest. Yet the din of the stalls swamps the readers settled at the far end, and children drifting between the tables unsettle anyone who came in search of quiet. The remedy brought in since autumn deserves praise. Nothing weighty has gone up: the nave is now broken by thick curtains, hung on rails and slid about as the hours require. The place breathes at last. It gains in gentleness what it loses in purity, and that owned-up flaw beats the fine idea that made the building unliveable.

units: the writer compares two systems for collecting waste
the first solution gives one bin to each home
this first solution is expensive to maintain
it makes sorting mistakes easy to trace
the second solution is a shared container sunk below ground
this container costs less and holds the smell in
its anonymity encourages illegal dumping
the writer recommends the second solution with clear signage
the decision will be taken at a coming residents' meeting
text: Here is my answer about the two waste systems our building is weighing up. The first gives every flat a bin of its own, emptied each week by the contractor. Upkeep costs a fair amount, though nobody can hide behind anyone else, since a sorting mistake can be traced back. The second comes far cheaper: everything drops into one shared container sunk below ground, on the strip of land beside the car park. It holds a great deal and the lid keeps the smell in, but anonymity invites illegal dumping. Set side by side, the two come down to this: one mends habits, the other mends clutter. Our real headache remains the bags piling up by the entrance, so I lean towards the sunken container, provided we put up signage anyone can read. Tell me what you think before the residents' meeting.

units: the head of an urban service is questioned about the public consultation
she believes the consultation brings incompatible uses to light
three subjects come back at almost every meeting
people living nearby want calmer traffic
shopkeepers fear a fall in custom
noise complaints clash with the need for places open late
outdoor tables cut into the room left for people on foot
the head denies that the consultation settles the disagreements
the final decision rests with the elected members
text: Asked what a public consultation is actually good for, the head of the urban service replies that it brings uses that clash with one another into the open. Three subjects come back, she notes, at almost every meeting. The first is traffic: people living nearby press for calmer roads, while shopkeepers dread a fall in custom. The second covers the hours after dark; against complaints about noise she sets the need for places that stay open late for the young. The third touches the pavement, where outdoor tables cut into the room left for pushchairs and wheelchairs. Does the consultation settle any of it? Not at all, she answers, and she does not dress the matter up. It gives the disagreements shape, puts them in order of weight, and leaves the elected members to carry the burden of choosing.

units: the chair of an association asks a volunteer about the state of the entrance hall
the volunteer reports overflowing letterboxes and parcels on the floor
the caretaker has been off sick for a fortnight
no stand-in has been arranged
one tenant had already given warning in writing without any reply
the treasurer suggests paying for a temporary replacement
the tenant objects that the fund is meant for something else
the chair decides to call round at the flats the next day
a general meeting will be called if nobody comes forward
text: As the meeting drew towards its close, the chair of the association asked the young volunteer what he had come across in the entrance hall. The letterboxes were overflowing, he said, and parcels had been lying on the floor since the day before. The chair wanted to know what lay behind such unusual disorder. The caretaker had been off sick for a fortnight, the volunteer explained, and nobody had been put in his place. One tenant added that she had already given warning in writing and had heard nothing back. The treasurer suggested paying for a temporary replacement as a one-off; the tenant objected that the fund was meant for something else. The chair settled the matter there and then: he would call round at the flats the next day, then summon a general meeting if nobody came forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: streets did not carry a displayed name from the outset
people once found their way by signs and shops
such bearings were enough while the neighbourhood stayed small
the spread of the outskirts made spoken directions useless
the authorities could no longer collect the taxes
they could no longer trace the people they were after
numbering house fronts grew out of that difficulty
the postman's round follows from it as well
residents objected to the measure at first
they saw it as an intrusion into their private life
text: Believe it or not, streets did not always carry a name on a plate for anyone to read. People once found their way by painted signs and shopfronts: you lived by the well, or across from the tanner, and that did the job well enough while the neighbourhood came down to no more than a handful of lanes. Then the outskirts spread, newcomers crowded in, and directions passed from door to door stopped working. The authorities moved for a very down-to-earth reason: they could no longer gather the taxes owed to them, nor lay hands on the people they were after. That is where numbered house fronts come from, and with them the postman's regular round. The odd part of the story is that residents kicked against the change at first: an address imposed on them felt like a trespass on their private life.

units: a rumour of a break-in goes round a residents' messaging group
the message is twisted and blown up within an evening
an alarming story travels faster than a denial
fear drives people to warn those close to them
setting the facts straight calls for patient enquiry
neighbourhood groups appoint two people to check
these checkers vet every alert before it goes out
a pause is imposed before anything is shared
the number of alerts falls and trust grows
text: A rumour swells in the residents' messaging group: intruders are said to have been through the basement. Within one evening the message is passed on, twisted and blown up. Researchers who study the way information travels know the pattern well enough. An alarming story travels faster than a denial, because it works on fear, and fear drives each of us to warn the people close to us. A single message rouses a whole building, whereas setting the facts straight calls for patient enquiry. Neighbourhood groups here and there are trying out a guard that works. They appoint two people to vet every alert before it goes out, and they impose a pause before anything is shared. The upshot of it all is striking: the alerts fall away, trust climbs back, and the exchanges take on some real use again.

units: the narrator watches two queues in a single week
the first stands at an official counter
this first queue stays silent and packed tight
everyone in it guards the place they hold
the second queue waits outside a volunteer-run canteen
people there talk loudly
they keep the place of a neighbour who has stepped away
the difference comes neither from the wait nor from the conditions outside
it rests on what each person hopes for at the head of the queue
text: I came across two crowds in the space of a single week, and nothing about them was alike. The first was waiting at an official counter: packed tight, silent, shuffling on the spot under a canopy that was far too short, each of them keeping an eye on the place they had won. Nothing passed between them but sighs and sidelong glances, as though waiting there forbade speech. The second had formed outside a volunteer-run canteen open to all. It shuffled on just as much, under the very same drizzle, yet voices carried, and people held the place of a neighbour who had gone off to fetch an umbrella. The gap had nothing to do with the length of the wait or with the weather. It rested on what each of them hoped for at the head of the queue: a refusal at one, hot soup and a familiar face at the other.

units: the procedure applies before an association's premises open to the public
the width of the entrance door must be measured
the slope of the ramp must be checked
a wheelchair must be able to turn without an awkward manoeuvre
the emergency exits must be found and kept clear
the charge in the extinguishers and the electrical inspection are to be checked
the furniture must be entered in a register with its condition
seats whose base gives way are to be taken out
a felt panel cures the echo of a bare ceiling
the compliance papers are to be asked of the owner after a refurbishment
text: Before an association's premises open to the public, work through these checks in the order given. Start with access: measure the width of the entrance door, check the slope of the ramp, make sure a wheelchair turns without an awkward manoeuvre. Move on to safety: find the emergency exits, clear them, check the charge in the extinguishers and the inspection of the electrical board. Then deal with the furniture: enter every chair and table in a register, note its condition, and take out anything whose base has given way. Finish with the acoustics, which tend to be forgotten: a bare ceiling throws voices back and makes talking a strain, whereas a felt panel is enough to cure the fault. If the building has been refurbished lately, ask the owner for the compliance papers and file them with the register.

units: a work-integration association applied to occupy an empty warehouse
the warehouse belongs to a public landlord
the application went unanswered at first
a technical meeting brought together the landlord, the safety officers and the people behind the scheme
the scheme planned a repair workshop and a shared kitchen
the experts demanded that the roof structure be strengthened
the landlord agreed to pay for that strengthening
the association undertook to handle upkeep and keep watch over the place
the agreement was signed at the end of autumn
a neighbouring building is now the subject of a similar request
text: It began when a work-integration association applied for temporary use of an empty warehouse held by a public landlord. The application went unanswered at first. A fortnight later a technical meeting brought together the landlord, the safety officers and the people behind the scheme, who hoped to put a repair workshop and a shared kitchen into the building. The experts found that the roof structure needed strengthening; without that, opening to the public was out of the question. The landlord offered a compromise: it would pay for the reinforcement, while the association would handle day-to-day upkeep and keep watch over the place. The agreement was signed at the end of autumn. The workshop has opened since, and the building next door, empty as well, is now the subject of a similar request.
